claims.text: High-entropy alloys typically exhibit high configurational disorder.
High-entropy alloys commonly have FCC or BCC structures.

A machine-learning model using local-lattice-distortion, atomic-mass-variance, and mixing-entropy descriptors will predict low phonon thermal conductivity more accurately than traditional empirical or physics-based models.
Atomic mass variance enhances phonon scattering in high-entropy alloys.
Local lattice distortions enhance phonon scattering in high-entropy alloys.
High configurational entropy induces local lattice distortions.
Inherent lattice disorder in high-entropy alloys increases phonon scattering.
Increased phonon scattering reduces phonon thermal conductivity.
Descriptors of mass mismatch and lattice distortion allow a machine-learning model to capture disorder-related scattering mechanisms.
Traditional predictive models rely on averaged or simplified parameters that inadequately account for local disorder in high-entropy alloys.
The proposed model will achieve a statistically significant reduction in prediction error relative to current empirical or physics-based approaches.
The proposed model will reduce prediction error by approximately 20% or more relative to current approaches.
The proposed model will improve identification of high-entropy alloys with ultralow phonon thermal conductivity.
The approach is applicable to single-phase solid-solution high-entropy alloys in which disorder-driven phonon scattering dominates thermal-conductivity reduction.
Multiphase high-entropy alloys may lie outside the model's valid range.
High-entropy alloys with significant clustering may lie outside the model's valid range.
Materials with substantial electronic contributions to total thermal conductivity may lie outside the model's valid range.
The model's transferability to high-entropy alloys deviating from well-ordered FCC or BCC configurations is uncertain.
